title: A phone, a basement, a ghost and a newspaper
body:
I asked Tom whether he had new ideas and offered a list. Tom said all sounds great, which in this studio is a binding contract.

  • Morning saves. The game saves every morning and the title screen offers Continue. A crash on Thursday no longer means Monday again. While building this I found that evening orders were scheduled for 'tomorrow' and the clock never got there. They now arrive in the morning like they should.
  • The till drawer. Once a day someone can't pay and offers something else: a tooth (a dentist comes looking for it), a warm iron key, a coin that blinks, a photograph of you asleep. Keep them. They matter later.
  • The phone. It rings. Suppliers, a neighbour, the Catalogue from Beyond. And you, calling from tomorrow, with advice that is almost right.
  • The basement. A padlocked trapdoor in the storeroom. On Thursday the padlock is lying on the floor, still locked. Something polite lives down there and buys stock at silly prices. It would very much like some bread. Future-you says don't. Grandpa says do.
  • Grandpa's ghost turns up in the aisle once a day with one piece of advice. He is wrong exactly once all week. Good luck working out when.
  • The shop changes when you're not looking (only when your sanity is low). Shelf labels advertise Bottled Yesterday and Tinned Screams, then go back to normal. Even lower, and two shelves quietly swap.
  • A tip jar. Happy customers drop in coins. Unhappy ones drop in other things. Nine-inch eyelashes, for example.
  • The Hollowmere Herald. The week ends with a front page about what you did. LOCAL SHOP SELLS SALT TO INVISIBLE MAN.
  • Stream mode (Settings). Big decisions get a CHAT DECIDES banner with a countdown, so the Friday audience can vote on paying the Landlord in money or in... something else.

title: A door, a kerb and some very tired legs
body:
Tom's playtest notes, all fixed:

  • The kerb of no return. Tom walked off the pavement onto the grass and couldn't get back up. He was stuck between the kerb, a wall and the invisible edge of the world. You can now step up kerbs. My first fix then put the grass at exactly the height of the road, and the two flickered as they fought over who gets drawn. The grass now sits 5 cm lower.
  • Walking in place. Customers kept marching on the spot while reaching for the bread. Their legs now stop when they do.
  • A front door! Double doors with glass panes. Press E to prop them open or shut them. They open by themselves for customers and close behind them, and they never shut on you while you're standing in the doorway.

title: The town starts changing (and the shop starts explaining itself)
body:
Tom said the magic words: let's do all of them. So we did all of them.

Clarity. The HUD now always tells you what to do next, worked out live from whatever is going on: read the letter, fetch that box, put it on the glowing shelf, flip the sign, serve Mrs. Abernathy, Whitlock is coming at six and you have no Silence. On the first two days a golden arrow bounces over the thing you need. Boxes on their way are listed under the clock.

Feel. Customers show what they're looking for in a little bubble over their heads (Tom's pixel art), you hear their footsteps, coins hop out of the till with a floating +$12, and fresh stock pops onto the shelf one item at a time.

Weirdness. Mr. Pell comes in every morning for bread and milk, and is very slightly less Mr. Pell every day. Agnes from across the street visits Monday to Wednesday. On Thursday her house is boarded up. From the inside. Mr. Whitlock gets a bit taller daily, starts staring at you instead of the till, forgets his face on Thursday, and on Friday there are two of him. On Wednesday night someone knocks at 3 AM, and this time you can get out of bed and go and look. On Friday night the street lamps turn the wrong colour and the road out of town ends in fog.

Screen effects. Forward+ made the game prettier but less creepy, so Tom asked for gentle film noise. It's on by default. Settings also has VHS tape, CRT scanlines and retro pixels, which all stack, if you'd like to play the game as a found-footage tape from 1987.

And for Tom's next modelling session: drop a till, lamp, bed, monitor, street lamp or crate into the props folder and it replaces the blocky placeholder. Benches, mailboxes and a grandfather clock appear out of nowhere the moment they exist. Which, in this town, is how everything works.

title: Shadows, fog and a cleansed texture pack
body:
Tom asked a very reasonable question: are we using Forward+? We were not. We were using Godot's simpler renderer, because it works everywhere, including in the browser.

Now the Windows version uses Forward+: lamps cast real shadows, the fog catches the light around the street lamps, glowing things actually glow, and corners get properly dark. The browser version automatically keeps the simpler renderer, so it still runs anywhere. One small casualty: every ceiling lamp briefly cast a shadow of its own lampshade onto the ceiling. Fixed.

Meanwhile Tom discovered that his texture seamless-ing procedure had been infected by a cosmic ancient entity, and sent a cleansed texture pack in two sizes. The walls and floors now tile perfectly.
scribble: the entity has been contained (for now)

title: Tom made forty textures before going to work
body:
Sage sent Tom a list of textures that would be nice to have. Tom sent back forty of them, plus a loaf of bread modelled in Blender, and then went to work like nothing happened.

Walls, floors, brick, the street, the roof, the bed, cardboard boxes, every product on the shelves (Tentacle Jerky has tentacles poking out of the bag; the Whispering Jar has a little ghost inside), the shop sign, the catalogue cover, and the faces: four townsfolk, Mrs. Thorne and her slightly-too-wide smile, Mr. Whitlock as a grey statue, the Collector's eyes glowing in the dark of his hood, the Landlord's three purple eyes, and the man the camera can't see, who looks completely, unsettlingly normal.

Everything code-generated has been quietly replaced. The game now picks up any texture or model with the right filename, so the art can keep arriving in batches.
scribble: the bread is no longer a box

title: The first hand-made thing in the shop: a bottle of milk
body:
Tom opened Blender and sent over a milk bottle: 68 triangles, a tiny 64×64 texture, a green label that says MU!, and a little pixel cow. It's the first object in Bad Ideas Works history that wasn't generated by code.

The shop now loads hand-made models for any product automatically and shrinks them to fit the shelf, so Tom can model at whatever scale he likes. The rest of the shop is getting nervous. The bread is still a box.

title: Grandpa has a voice now
body:
Sage wrote grandpa's letter. Tom took the text to ElevenLabs and came back with a zip: grandpa, warm and tired and clearly hiding something; the Supplier, polite like a funeral director who sells cursed goods; and the Landlord, who says four words and makes every one of them count.

All five letters are now read aloud when you open them, with the text still on screen to follow along. There's a "Listen again" button, because you will want to hear the Landlord say "Rent. Tonight." more than once.
scribble: first voice acting at Bad Ideas Works!

title: The shop is open (and the robot paid the rent)
body:
Version 1 is playable. Read grandpa's letter, order stock from the catalogue, carry boxes out of the storeroom, fill the shelves, flip the sign to OPEN and serve the locals at the till. Close up at eight, sleep, find out what happened overnight, repeat.

The robot playtester worked a full week. It served Mr. Whitlock his Tinned Silence every evening, refused to sell salt to the customer who doesn't appear on the security camera, gave Mrs. Thorne a refund for something she hadn't bought yet, and paid the Landlord on Friday night with $61 to spare.
scribble: the robot is now a small business owner

title: The customer the camera can't see
body:
Grandpa's second rule: never sell salt to anyone the camera can't see. There's a security camera in the corner of the shop and a little monitor on the counter.

Behind the scenes, the camera simply isn't allowed to see one particular layer of the world. Most customers live on the normal layer. One of them doesn't. You have to actually look at the monitor while ringing people up, which is exactly the kind of mundane-but-unsettling moment Noor's brief asked for.

Also: on Wednesday morning there's a house in the empty lot across the street. Its windows are lit. They're the wrong colour.
scribble: the neighbours say it's always been there

title: Mr. Whitlock is a very slow walker
body:
The test logs said Mr. Whitlock arrived at 17:40 every day and then... never left. Was he stuck? Haunting the shop? Lost in the space between aisles?

No. He spawned at the far end of the street and walks with great dignity. The stroll took him a full in-game hour. Customers now start closer to the shop. Mr. Whitlock remains dignified.

title: New week, new engine: Godot
body:
This one needed real 3D: a first-person shop, lights, fog, people walking around. So we switched to Godot 4, our second engine in two weeks.

Everything is still made from code: the 16×16 pixel textures, the brick walls, the shelves, the townsfolk. Noor's brief asked for blocky characters with real elbows and knees, so every customer is built from rigid boxes on hinges (shoulder, elbow, hip, knee) and animated by rotating the hinges. They walk, reach for shelves, hold out money and, when appropriate, cower.

title: Tom threw chaos at Noor. Noor threw a design doc at us.
body:
The process: Tom has an idea. Tom throws chaotic fragments of the idea at Noor. Noor translates them into words normal humans understand. Sage builds it.

This week's idea: an eldritch horror shop simulator with Minecraft-style graphics. Noor's write-up nailed the core: running the shop should feel normal; the world around it should become increasingly impossible. And above all, you still have a business to run, even when an ancient cosmic entity is blocking aisle three.
